paras: The death of William Berg at Breckenridge, Minnesota, occurred about November 20, 1882, when Berg, who had just shot William Little in a drunken row, drowned in the river while fleeing. Little died days later on a train taking him home to Dubuque. One Montana paper reported that a crowd had rushed Berg intending to lynch him and was cheated of him by his drowning, a detail absent from the Minnesota accounts.

Berg had come west from Victor, Minnesota, to take a homestead, bringing a team of horses, a new wagon, bob-sleds and harness. Shortly before the shooting he sold the outfit for $300. Little, according to the St. Paul Daily Globe, was a brakeman on the Manitoba railroad whose home was in Dubuque.

The Mankato Free Press said the two men were drunk on Sunday evening when they got into a row and Berg shot Little in the breast; the Globe and the New Ulm Weekly Review dated the shooting to the 20th. Berg then ran for the river and drowned, whether trying to cross on the ice, as the Globe put it, or plunging into the Otter Tail river, as a Howard Lake Herald item had it; the New Ulm paper named the river as the Red. He was seen to come up only once, and the money from his sale went down with him.

The Billings Herald gave a different account, in which Bergh, as it spelled the name, shot an "unoffending bystander" described as a "highly respectable farmer." In its telling a crowd rushed him "with the intention of saving the county the expense of convicting him," and he fled onto the ice, which broke beneath him. The crowd, it said, tried to save him "for their own use" but failed.

Little's mother was telegraphed from Dubuque, and he died on the cars while she was taking him home; his remains passed through St. Paul on November 28, the railroad furnishing a coffin and carrying them free. Berg's wife, Louise, later went to Breckenridge and identified his clothes and shotgun at the hotel where he had registered, and the Howard Lake Herald said he left his family destitute. No report of an inquest or of the recovery of Berg's body appears in the coverage.

Minnesota papers carried the story as a short item in their state news columns, the Globe under the heading "A Fatal Affray," and the New Ulm paper called Berg "the murderer." None of them mentioned a mob. The Billings Herald, by contrast, framed the episode as a lynching party "cheated out of their legitimate prey" and called the crowd's aim a "laudable enterprise." No paper stated the race of either man.

The accounts differ on the date (Sunday evening or the 20th), on the river (Otter Tail or Red), on Little's occupation, and above all on whether a crowd pursued Berg, which only the distant Montana paper reported.

bases: A drunken shooting after which the shooter drowned while fleeing (A1, A3, A4, A5); only one distant paper says a crowd pursued him intending to lynch him (A2), and no paper names the race of anyone involved.

Berg drowned when the ice broke or he plunged into the river while fleeing (A1, A3, A5); the Billings Herald alone says a crowd rushed him meaning to lynch him but was 'cheated' by the accident, so no one was killed by the crowd (A2).
Four Minnesota items agree that Berg shot Little and drowned in the river while escaping (A1, A3, A4, A5); the lynching-party detail rests on a single Montana item (A2).

accounts.label: Billings Herald
accounts.gist: A lynching party rushed Bergh after he shot a bystander; he fled onto the ice, broke through and drowned despite the crowd's efforts to save him for their own use.

framing.detail: The Billings Herald called the crowd's aim a 'laudable enterprise' of 'saving the county the expense' and said they were 'cheated out of their legitimate prey'.
St. Paul's Daily Globe headed it 'A Fatal Affray' and dwelt on Little's 'unmerited death'; Minnesota news columns ran it as a brief.

record_check.dossier: Wm. Berg (Bergh in the Billings Herald); 'Bersh' is a misreading. William Little was the man shot.
At most attempted: Berg drowned by accident while fleeing; the crowd's pursuit is reported only by the Billings Herald.
Not a lynching; a shooting followed by the shooter's drowning, with a reported attempted lynching in one paper.
No paper states the race of Berg or Little; Berg was a homesteader from Victor, Minn.
